Introduction

Hi, I’m
Scott Shen.

I’m a junior at Marquette High School in Ballwin, Missouri. I want to work in public policy so I can help the most vulnerable people in the United States live better lives.

My school day tends to spill past the final bell. One afternoon I’m debating who should pay for health insurance. The next, I’m questioning a mock trial witness. And on the weekends, I'm proposing a start-up-business plan to my DECA judges.

Explore my philosophy

What guides me

My core values

Curiosity

I value curiosity because I believe there is always more to understand about the world around me. Rather than accepting things at face value, I find meaning in asking why and allowing the answers to reshape the way I see the world.

Advocacy

I value advocacy because I believe that recognizing an issue means little if we are unwilling to act upon it. To me, advocacy is about using my voice to bring attention to the experiences of others and contribute to meaningful change beyond myself.

Initiative

I value initiative because I believe that meaningful change begins with the willingness to take the first step. Rather than waiting for opportunities to present themselves, I strive to create them through purposeful action.

Philosophy

The gift of education

As a kid, my dad always told me to value every opportunity to learn something new. Now that i'm older, I can see why my education is the only true gift.

On this page

Education as a GiftLearning as a Lifelong PursuitKnowledge as a Responsibility

Education as a Gift

I believe education is the only true gift in life. Unlike material possessions, education gives us something that cannot be taken away: the ability to understand the world around us and envision what it could become. Every opportunity to learn is an opportunity to expand our perspectives and discover possibilities we never knew existed. To receive an education is a privilege, and I believe that such a privilege should never go to waste.

Learning as a Lifelong Pursuit

To me, education extends far beyond the confines of a classroom. It is not simply a pursuit of academic excellence, but a lifelong commitment to understanding the unknown. I believe curiosity is at the heart of a meaningful education, and that every experience, regardless of how ordinary it may seem, offers something worth learning. I aspire to approach life with the understanding that no amount of knowledge should ever diminish our desire to learn more.

Knowledge as a Responsibility

The true value of education lies not in the knowledge we accumulate, but in what we choose to do with it. I believe that receiving the gift of education comes with a responsibility to make a meaningful difference in the lives of others. Education should empower us not only to recognize the shortcomings of our world but also to take the initiative to address them. Ultimately, I aspire to live a life in which my education serves a purpose greater than my own success.

Armstrong Teasdale internship

A summer behind the scenes

In summer 2026, the St. Louis Internship Program placed me in Records Management at Armstrong Teasdale. Most people picture a law firm and picture a courtroom. I spent my summer learning about everything that has to happen before a courtroom is even possible, and I believe that side of the work matters just as much.

Where a record goes

Mock Trial usually hands me a packet with everything already in it. Armstrong Teasdale showed me where that packet comes from. I learned how a record is stored, how someone finds the right one years later, and how its path through the firm gets traced. A case is only as strong as the file underneath it, and being able to explain a piece of evidence starts with being able to put a hand on it.

Back at Marquette

When I prepare for debate now, I think about my partner. If he needs the source behind a claim in the middle of a round, he cannot wait for me to go looking for it. Organization is not the exciting part of advocacy. It is the part everything else stands on, and I did not understand that until I watched professionals depend on it every day.

Looking ahead

My dream is to study economics at NYU. I want to study a subway fare increase in class and then hear from the people actually paying it on my ride home, because a policy is never only a number. I also want to become a lawyer and bring that training into public policy. I want to sit down with someone, understand how a rule is affecting their life, and make the case for changing it.

Speech & Debate

Overview

I am captain of Speech & Debate at Marquette, and I compete in Congressional Debate and Policy Debate. The two events are very different, but both ask the same question: what does this proposal mean for the people it affects? That question follows me from school funding bills to health insurance debates, and it is the question I care about most.

Congressional Debate

In Congressional Debate, everything comes down to three minutes. One bill I worked on would fund cleaner public schools. Preparing both sides meant asking which problems a grant could actually fix for a teacher or a student, because a bill that sounds good in a speech still has to work in a building. Three minutes is not a lot of time, so every sentence has to earn its place.

Policy Debate

My partner and I developed a proposal for national catastrophic health insurance. The hardest line to write was the one about the deductible. Changing a percentage on our page changed what a family would have to pay, and once I understood that, I could not treat any line in the plan as just a line. That is the kind of detail that got me interested in public policy.

Mock Trial

In Dragons' Bay, I prepared to cross-examine an engineering expert about a log flume incident. I kept asking the same two questions. Which parts of this testimony came from firsthand observation? Which parts were inferences? I also earned Best Witness at Missouri Mock Trial in 2026. Sitting on both sides of the questioning, asking and answering, is part of why I want to practice law.

Model United Nations

As a Model UN officer, I get to work on a different side of public speaking. Representing Sierra Leone on the Rohingya refugee crisis meant I had to understand the position of the country I represented before I could ask another delegate to work with me. Persuasion works differently when the position is not your own. First you learn what the other side needs. Then you negotiate.

American Legion Oratorical Contest

The American Legion Contest means alot to me. Speaking about the Constitution pushes me to explain why my government matters to someone who has never had to memorize it for class. It tests my knowledge of this wonderful country because if I cannot explain it in plain language, I probably do not understand it well enough myself.

Future Business Leaders of America

As a vice president of Marquette FBLA, I have worked on chapter events and studied parliamentary procedure. I like the practical side of those rules. A member with an idea needs to know how to get it on the floor and how to call for a vote, and procedure is what makes that possible. Without it, the loudest voice wins. With it, the best idea can.

DECA

In Sports & Entertainment Marketing Series, I work through a business problem and present my recommendation to a judge playing the role of an investor. The Start-Up Business Plan event is a secret for now. My teammate and I are building something we believe could change how students experience a class, and the details stay between us and a growing stack of drafts until the plan is ready for this great blue marble we call the world. Some ideas are just worth keeping quiet until they are ready.

National Honor Society

I was inducted into Marquette's National Honor Society in 2026. Service is the part of that recognition I want to carry into my career. Institutions are hard to navigate from the outside, and I want to be someone who helps people find their way through one, especially when the process was never explained to them.

Science National Honor Society

I am a member of Science National Honor Society at Marquette. What draws me to science is figuring out how to answer a question with evidence. I wondered what the word "natural" on a cleaner's label could tell me about how well it worked. To explore that question, I compared tea tree oil with 70% isopropyl alcohol and looked at where bacteria grew and where they did not. The label made a claim. The experiment gave me a way to check it.

Science Bowl

I am a Science Bowl co-captain. I like how differently a team has to listen here than in debate. In debate, I argue for my own reading of the question. In Science Bowl, a teammate might recognize the physics behind a question before I have even figured out what it is asking, and my job is to trust that and let their answer stand.

DECA Start-Up Business Plan

This one is a secret. My teammate and I are writing a business plan for something we believe could change how a student experiences a class, and we are not telling anyone what it is. The details stay between us and a growing stack of drafts. It started with a frustration every student has felt, the kind everyone assumes cannot be fixed. We disagreed.

The research came first, and what came out of it is something we believe in completely. When it is finally ready for this great blue marble we call the world, it will not sound like anything else in the room. Until then, we keep building in the dark. Some ideas are just too perfect to announce before their time. Check back after competition season.

The efficacy of natural cleaning solutions

I compared tea tree oil with 70% isopropyl alcohol to see how well each inhibited E. coli K-12 in a lab setting, measuring the areas where bacteria did not grow around each sample.

Amazon rainforest research

My paper, "The Cultural Effects of Deforestation in the Amazon Rainforest on Indigenous Tribes," asked what forest loss means for the people who call the Amazon home.
